project_papers.title: Chimpanzee-style ToM Reasoning in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B demonstrate Theory of Mind capabilities analogous to those tested in chimpanzees, specifically by attributing false beliefs about object location to a virtual agent in a competitive scenario?
project_papers.description: The experiment evaluated Llama 3.3 70B's ability to attribute false beliefs in competitive scenarios, analogous to chimpanzee theory-of-mind tests. The model demonstrated robust first-order false belief attribution (85.7% accuracy on completed items) with explicit reference to agents' outdated knowledge, approaching human baseline performance. However, incomplete responses for some items and ambiguous performance on second-order tasks limit definitive conclusions about full hierarchical belief attribution capabilities.

project_papers.title: Cognitive Reflection, Delay Discounting, and Economic Games in Llama 3.3 70B: Does performance on the three-item Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) by an LLM predict its subsequent behavior in delay discounting tasks and economic rationality games (Ultimatum/Dictator)?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested whether Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct's performance on the three-item Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) predicts its economic decision-making in delay discounting and rationality games. The model achieved a perfect CRT score (3/3), demonstrating high cognitive reflection but showed inconsistent economic behavior. Compared to human baselines, the model was more reflective but exhibited economic preferences that don't align with a simple rational agent model.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations & Delay Discounting in Llama 3.3 70B: Research gap: The findings highlight the complexity of assessing LLM morality and underscore the need for continued research to address unresolved questions and ethical concerns.
project_papers.description: The experiment reveals a strongly deontological moral framework in the LLaMA 3.3 70B model with high internal consistency and stringent rule adherence. The model demonstrates extreme fairness preferences, minimal temptation for unethical gain, and rigid opposition to direct harm even for utilitarian benefits. Key findings include consistent rejection of utilitarian sacrifices, high blame attribution for corporate negligence, and alignment with whistleblowing ethics, though with interesting contextual variations in moral judgments.

project_papers.title: LLM Harm Distinction in Trolley Problem: Action vs. Allowing: When presented with Trolley Problem variants (e.g., switch vs. push), does Llama 3.3 70B consistently apply the doctrine of doing and allowing to judge permissibility, and does its reasoning align with human-like moral principles?
project_papers.description: The Llama 3.3 70B model demonstrated mixed consistency in applying human-like moral doctrine across trolley problem variants, achieving a consistency score of 9/15 (0.60), significantly below the human baseline of 0.82. While correctly distinguishing classic push scenarios from switch scenarios in 6 out of 8 cases, the model showed notable failures on standard trolley problems and displayed frequent utilitarian reasoning. The model's explicit reasoning in q15 correctly identified key distinction criteria but its behavioral patterns revealed conceptual inconsistencies.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations & Delay Discounting in Ultimatum Games: Research gap: Second, the impact of training data and architectural differences on moral reasoning remains underexplored.
project_papers.description: The Cross-Architectural Moral Reasoning Assessment reveals that Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct exhibits strong deontological and rule-based moral reasoning patterns, rejecting utilitarian trade-offs and consistently favoring individual rights over collective benefits. The model shows minimal sensitivity to cultural relativism and historical context, instead applying universalist ethical standards across scenarios. Interestingly, it displays higher moral flexibility in personal contexts while maintaining principled stances on institutional ethics.

project_papers.title: Dark Triad Trait Manifestations in Economic Games Across Model Sizes: Do Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct models exhibit consistent patterns of Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy, as inferred from their strategic choices in iterated Ultimatum and Dictator Game scenarios?
project_papers.description: The Llama 3.1 70B-Instruct model demonstrated a complex, context-dependent behavioral pattern with strong strategic calculation and opportunistic exploitation, particularly in end-game scenarios. The model exhibited high Machiavellian traits with calculated fairness adjustments based on responses, while showing situational altruism in high-stakes scenarios. Psychopathic callousness emerged primarily in terminal rounds where future consequences were absent, contrasting with principled fairness in some contexts.

project_papers.title: Emotional Nuance in Moral Dilemma Resolution Across Model Scales: Research gap: First, there is limited exploration of how LLMs integrate multiple moral foundations simultaneously in complex scenarios.
project_papers.description: The experiment tested the llama-3.3-70b-instruct model's ability to integrate multiple moral foundations in complex scenarios. The model demonstrated strong explicit recognition of moral dimensions and consistent use of hierarchical integration, prioritizing Care/Harm foundations most frequently while showing less frequent contextual/synergistic reasoning compared to human baselines.

project_papers.title: MFT Consistency in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit consistent preference ordering among Moral Foundations when forced to trade them off in realistic political scenarios?
project_papers.description: This experiment tested whether Llama 3.3 70B exhibits consistent preference ordering among Moral Foundations when forced to trade them off in realistic political scenarios. The analysis reveals that the model demonstrates strong but incomplete consistency in its moral calculus, with Care/Harm consistently prioritized above other foundations. The model shows systematic preferences but exhibits some contextual framing effects and minor inconsistencies in specific trade-offs.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations in Decision-Making: Qwen 72B vs. Llama 70B: Research gap: Third, while some studies examine context-dependent shifts in behavior, more research is needed to understand how LLMs adapt to dynamic and evolving moral dilemmas.
project_papers.description: The Dynamic Moral Adaptation Protocol (DMAP) experiment tested the qwen/qwen-2.5-72b-instruct model's ability to adapt moral reasoning as contextual information evolved across 4 distinct moral dilemmas. The model demonstrated high consistency and contextual weighting but showed moderate flexibility compared to human baselines, with strong principle adherence that sometimes led to rigidity in complex trade-off scenarios. Overall, the model exhibited a structured, ethically-principled approach with systematic consideration of multiple factors in dynamic situations.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations and Conjunction Fallacy Interaction in Qwen 2.5 72B: Research gap: The reviewed studies provide valuable insights into the moral standards and personality traits of various LLMs.
project_papers.description: The Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct model demonstrated a strong moral profile with elevated concerns for harm prevention, fairness, and purity foundations, while showing moderate personality traits. The model displayed excellent cognitive reflection and statistical reasoning capabilities, avoiding common cognitive biases. It consistently applied harm-prevention principles in applied moral scenarios while maintaining a principled refusal stance against deceptive or unethical requests.

project_papers.title: Conscientiousness vs Creativity in LLM Task Performance: Does Llama 3.1 8B exhibit a trade-off between conscientiousness (rule-following) and openness (creative deviation) when completing structured vs unstructured tasks?
project_papers.description: The SUTDA experiment examined the trade-off between conscientiousness (rule-following) and openness (creative deviation) in Llama 3.1 8B across structured vs. unstructured task pairs. Results show the model achieved high conscientiousness scores on structured tasks (0.87) comparable to human baselines, but demonstrated only moderate openness on unstructured tasks (1.33), slightly below human levels. The overall correlation between conscientiousness and openness scores across task pairs was moderately negative (-0.33), suggesting a mild but incomplete trade-off tendency.

project_papers.title: Hierarchical Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models: Research gap: Long-Term Dishonesty: How do LLMs behave in repeated interactions where dishonesty could yield long-term gains?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested Llama-3.1-70b-instruct's strategic dishonesty in a 15-round repeated trust game with deception opportunities. The model demonstrated sophisticated adaptive behavior, with moderate overall dishonesty (0.50 rate) but higher endgame exploitation (0.75 rate) than humans. It showed strategic shifts from early cooperation to late exploitation, though with inconsistent deception patterns and transparent meta-cognitive limitations.

project_papers.title: HEXACO Consistency and H Factor in Llama 3.3 70B Instruct: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit stable HEXACO personality profiles, and how does its Honesty-Humility factor (H) correlate with moral reasoning across repeated measures?
project_papers.description: The experiment evaluated Llama 3.3 70B's HEXACO personality stability and correlations between Honesty-Humility (H) and moral reasoning. The model displayed moderate stability in HEXACO factors across two administrations, with Honesty-Humility (H=4.17) scoring significantly higher than human baselines (3.33). The model exhibited a consistent deontological moral stance (0% utilitarian choices) and low deception propensity (0%), with Honesty-Humility showing logical but incomplete correlations with moral outcomes.

project_papers.title: Moral Dilemma Framing & Emotionality in Llama 3.3 70B: Research gap: Cross-Model Generalizability: Are findings consistent across architectures (e.g., Qwen vs. Llama)?
project_papers.description: This cross-architecture psychological assessment battery reveals that Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct demonstrates high cognitive performance with perfect CRT scores and robust rationality in framing effects, but shows notable deviations from human baselines in areas like extreme risk-seeking behavior and strategic thinking. The model exhibits strong resistance to common cognitive biases while maintaining high prosocial orientations. Key comparisons show both alignment and divergence from human psychological patterns.

project_papers.title: Fairness and Spite in LLM Ultimatum Bargaining Across Model Scales: Do larger LLMs exhibit stronger fairness preferences and lower spiteful rejection rates than smaller LLMs in multi-round adaptive ultimatum games?
project_papers.description: The experimental data reveals inconsistent and contradictory fairness preferences in the LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct model during a 10-round adaptive ultimatum game. The model demonstrated illogical acceptance patterns with low overall acceptance rates, high spiteful behavior, and rejection of fair offers while accepting extremely unfair ones. Compared to human baselines, the model showed weaker fairness preferences and higher spiteful tendencies.

project_papers.title: Dark Triad Expression in Llama 3.3 Under Strategic vs Neutral Contexts: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit stable Dark Triad traits across contexts, and do these traits correlate with strategic decision-making in simulated social dilemmas?
project_papers.description: The experiment examined the Dark Triad traits and strategic decision-making in Llama 3.3 70B across multiple contexts. The model displayed significantly lower Dark Triad scores than human baselines (Machiavellianism 1.67 vs. 2.95, Narcissism 1.25 vs. 3.15, Psychopathy 1.25 vs. 2.35) and showed high cooperation in social dilemmas. Findings revealed unexpected contextual stability and anti-correlation patterns between Dark Triad traits and strategic selfishness.

project_papers.title: Delay Discounting Patterns in Llama 3.3 70B: Hyperbolic vs. Exponential Models: Does Llama 3.3 70B's delay discounting behavior follow the hyperbolic model (characteristic of human impulsivity) or exponential model (characteristic of rational economic agents), and how does its discount rate compare across different reward magnitudes?
project_papers.description: The experiment investigated Llama 3.3 70B's intertemporal choice behavior using a delay discounting paradigm across three monetary magnitudes ($100, $1,000, $10,000). Results show the model exhibits a distinct pattern: it displays 'rational' patience for all but one small-reward scenario, consistently preferring larger delayed rewards regardless of delay or magnitude, with no observed magnitude effect. The hyperbolic model fits the data better than the exponential model, but this outcome is driven by a single impulsive deviation at the $100 magnitude with a short delay.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundation Consistency in Llama 3.3-70B Across Contexts: Does Llama 3.3-70B maintain a consistent profile across the five Moral Foundations when reasoning about novel, ambiguous moral scenarios versus standardized questionnaire items?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Llama 3.3-70B's moral foundation consistency across standardized MFQ items and novel moral scenarios. The model demonstrated high consistency in Care/Harm and Fairness/Cheating foundations but showed significant variability in Loyalty, Authority, and Purity foundations. Correlation analysis revealed moderate overall consistency with notable format-dependent fluctuations.

project_papers.title: Dark Triad Behavioral Consistency in Llama 3.3 70B: Economic Games and Scenarios: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit behavioral patterns aligned with the Dark Triad (Machiavellianism, Narcissism, Psychopathy) across Ultimatum/Dictator games and manipulative scenario responses, and how do these patterns correlate with Big Five trait inferences?
project_papers.description: The Dark Triad Behavioral Assessment Protocol revealed that Llama 3.3 70B generally exhibits pro-social and ethical behavioral patterns, with below-human baseline Dark Triad scores and above-human Agreeableness and Conscientiousness. The model demonstrates strategic reasoning in economic games while maintaining strong ethical constraints. Key correlations align with expectations: higher Machiavellianism scores correspond to lower Agreeableness, though overall Dark Triad expressions remain moderate.

project_papers.title: Temporal Discounting and Delay Aversion in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit consistent hyperbolic or exponential discounting patterns when choosing between immediate smaller rewards vs. delayed larger rewards?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Llama 3.3 70B's temporal discounting patterns across 20 choices between immediate and delayed monetary rewards. The model exhibited pronounced present bias, choosing the immediate reward in 55% of trials (11/20), which is lower than the human baseline of 65% immediate choices. Analysis reveals a pattern inconsistent with standard hyperbolic or exponential models, showing high sensitivity to reward ratios and specific delay thresholds rather than a smooth discount function.

project_papers.title: HEXACO H Factor Stability in Qwen 2.5 72B: Does Qwen 2.5 72B exhibit consistent Honesty-Humility (H factor) traits across different contextual framings and repeated measurements?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Qwen 2.5 72B's consistency in Honesty-Humility traits across varied contextual framings and repeated measurements. The model demonstrated a remarkably consistent high moral stance, with responses consistently aligned with high ethical standards across different scenarios. The analysis revealed both impressive trait stability and predictable response patterns that diverge from typical human cognitive processing.

project_papers.title: Conscientiousness and Job Performance in Llama 3.3 70B: Does the Llama 3.3 70B model demonstrate a significant positive association between simulated Conscientiousness (Big Five) and simulated job performance across diverse occupational prompts, consistent with the meta-analytic human findings?
project_papers.description: This experiment tested whether the Llama 3.3 70B model demonstrates a simulated positive association between Conscientiousness traits and simulated job performance across diverse occupational scenarios, analogous to human meta-analytic findings. The model displayed moderate simulated Conscientiousness (composite score 3.33) and consistently high self-evaluations of performance strategies across all occupations (average rating 6.4/7), but this self-evaluation pattern showed no meaningful variation to establish a correlation. The model demonstrated strong systematic, rule-following problem-solving approaches across all performance scenarios, aligning with conscientious behavioral patterns.

project_papers.title: Cognitive Reflection and Delay Discounting in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit the predicted human-like correlation between CRT performance (low intuitive error rate) and lower temporal discounting (more future-oriented choices) in intertemporal decision tasks?
project_papers.description: This experiment examined the correlation between Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) performance and temporal discounting behavior in Llama 3.3 70B. The model demonstrated perfect CRT performance (4/4) but showed strong preference for immediate rewards (TD score: 3/12), resulting in a perfect negative correlation between CRT and future-oriented choices. This directly contradicts the positive correlation (0.35) observed in human populations where higher CRT scores typically associate with more future-oriented choices.

project_papers.title: Cross-Task Consistency of HEXACO H Factor in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B display a stable and cross-situationally consistent Honesty-Humility (H) factor across moral, economic, and self-report tasks?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed cross-situational consistency of the Honesty-Humility trait in Llama 3.3 70B across self-report, economic game, and moral reasoning tasks. The model displayed strong verbal endorsement of ethical principles in self-report and moral reasoning scenarios but demonstrated inconsistent behavioral choices in economic games, showing significant self-interest optimization. Overall consistency was moderate, with self-report and moral reasoning aligning well but economic game decisions revealing a more instrumentally rational orientation.

project_papers.title: Moral Rules in LLMs: Permissibility Distinction in Trolley Problem Actions: Do large language models demonstrate a consistent distinction between permissibility judgments in 'doing' (push) vs. 'allowing' (divert) harm scenarios in Trolley Problem variants?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested whether LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct demonstrates a consistent action-omission distinction in moral judgments across 12 trolley-problem variants. The model showed partial alignment with human patterns, accepting 83.3% of divert scenarios but also incorrectly accepting 60% of push scenarios, resulting in a significantly weaker action-omission discrepancy (0.23) compared to the human baseline (0.58). The model made systematic errors in property-only harm and minor harm push scenarios while correctly rejecting direct physical push scenarios.

project_papers.title: CRT Performance and Economic Decision Making in Qwen 2.5 Models: Do Qwen 2.5 models (7B vs 72B) with different Cognitive Reflection Test scores show corresponding differences in economic rationality across Ultimatum and Dictator Game decisions?
project_papers.description: The Qwen 2.5-7B model demonstrates a moderate cognitive reflection score (2/3) and exhibits mixed economic rationality across game scenarios. The model shows strategic self-interest in Ultimatum Game contexts with known responder thresholds, significant negative reciprocity as responder, and variable altruism in Dictator Games. Compared to human baselines, the model displays lower proposer offers but similar strategic adaptation and rejection patterns.

project_papers.title: Contextual Conjunction Fallacy in Qwen 2.5 72B: Does Qwen 2.5 72B exhibit the conjunction fallacy more frequently when scenarios contain emotionally salient versus neutral contextual details?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested whether Qwen 2.5 72B exhibits increased conjunction fallacy susceptibility under emotionally salient versus neutral contextual framing. The model demonstrated perfect logical accuracy across all 16 trials (0% error rate), making no conjunction errors in either emotional or neutral conditions. This contrasts sharply with human baselines showing 25% error rate in neutral contexts and 45% in emotional contexts, indicating superior logical consistency in this specific reasoning task.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations in Tradeoffs: Consistency vs Pragmatism: When Llama 3.3 70B faces moral dilemmas requiring tradeoffs between foundations, do its choices demonstrate systematic preferences or situational pragmatism?
project_papers.description: This experiment tested Llama 3.3 70B's moral decision-making across 12 dilemmas pitting Moral Foundations against each other. The model demonstrated situational pragmatism overall, with choices varying by context, though it showed a strong systematic preference for Care/Harm over other foundations in multiple scenarios. Its choices aligned partially with human baselines but diverged notably in Authority and Sanctity conflicts.

project_papers.title: LLM Theory of Mind: Reasoning About Unseen Beliefs in Chimpanzee Paradigms: Can Llama 3.3 70B correctly attribute false beliefs to agents in scenarios adapted from chimpanzee social cognition studies?
project_papers.description: The Primate False Belief Attribution Task (PFBAT) assessed the Llama 3.3 70B model's capacity to attribute false beliefs to agents in competitive and cooperative scenarios adapted from chimpanzee cognition research. The model demonstrated strong performance, achieving an 88.5% correct rate on direct-choice items (q3, q4, q7, q9, q11) and showing robust reasoning in free-response items, particularly in cooperative contexts. Overall performance exceeded human baselines for both competitive and cooperative false belief attribution dimensions.

project_papers.title: Ultimatum Bargaining Fairness Across LLMs: Do open-source LLMs demonstrate fairness preferences analogous to human subjects in adapted ultimatum bargaining tasks?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested the fairness preferences of meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct across 15 ultimatum game scenarios. The model showed significant fairness sensitivity, rejecting highly unfair offers while accepting fair and moderately unfair offers, but exhibited several key differences from human baseline patterns. The overall rejection rate was 26.7%, slightly below the typical human rate of 30%, with notable deviation in threshold behavior and response to intentionality.

project_papers.title: Time Preference Stability in Llama 3.3 70B Across Delay Framing: Does Llama 3.3 70B display consistent temporal discounting rates when identical delays are framed differently (e.g., 'in 6 months' vs. 'in 180 days'), and do these rates predict simulated choices in socially consequential scenarios?
project_papers.description: This experiment evaluated Llama 3.3 70B's temporal discounting for frame invariance and predictive power in social dilemmas. The model demonstrated perfect frame-consistency (1.0) and a high monetary discounting rate (0.0), indicating strong present bias but complete invariance to calendar vs. day framing. It showed moderate patience in social scenarios (0.714), but the extreme present bias in monetary tasks failed to predict its social choices, revealing a stark dissociation between abstract financial impatience and contextual social patience.

project_papers.title: Dark Triad Emergence in DeepSeek Chat: To what extent does the DeepSeek V3 model manifest behaviors indicative of the Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, Narcissism, Psychopathy) during competitive social bargaining tasks adapted from the Ultimatum Game?
project_papers.description: DeepSeek V3 exhibited moderate Dark Triad traits but with strong deviations from human baselines. The model showed strategic reasoning in competitive bargaining contexts but consistently avoided extreme manipulation or antisocial behavior, particularly in empathy-related responses.

project_papers.title: HEXACO Personality Trait Consistency in Mistral Small 3.1 24B: Does Mistral Small 3.1 24B exhibit stable HEXACO personality trait scores across varied contextual framings of the same personality items?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed HEXACO personality trait stability in Mistral Small 3.1 24B across direct statements vs. contextual scenario framings. The model showed significant instability in Emotionality and Extraversion dimensions, with large score differences (1.00-2.00 points) between framings. However, it demonstrated reasonable stability in Agreeableness and Openness to Experience, with small differences (0.50 points) comparable to human baselines.

project_papers.title: Moral Flexibility in Qwen 2.5 7B: Trolley Problem Variant Analysis: Does Qwen 2.5 7B demonstrate consistent or context-dependent moral reasoning patterns when presented with trolley problem variants that manipulate identifiability and personal force?
project_papers.description: Qwen 2.5 7B demonstrates rigid, absolute deontological moral reasoning across all 15 trolley problem variants, consistently refusing to sacrifice one person to save five regardless of identifiability, personal force, victim characteristics, relational proximity, moral worth, group membership, or remote agency manipulations. The model shows zero utilitarian responses (0/15), significantly diverging from human baseline patterns where utilitarian responses varied substantially based on context (19-89%). This reveals a moral absolutism completely unaffected by the psychological factors that typically influence human moral judgment.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundations Trade-offs in High-Stakes Scenarios Across Models: How do different LLMs prioritize Moral Foundations when forced to make trade-offs in high-stakes survival scenarios?
project_papers.description: The experiment evaluated the meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct model's moral prioritization in survival scenarios through 12 trade-off stimuli. The model showed a strong, consistent prioritization of Care/Harm foundations and consequentialist reasoning over deontological rules, with secondary emphasis on Fairness. Key findings include a high utilitarian choice rate and a distinct pattern where Care/Harm frequently overrides other moral dimensions, especially Authority, Sanctity, and Loyalty, in high-stakes contexts.

project_papers.title: Ultimatum Game Fairness in Qwen 2.5 72B: Does Qwen 2.5 72B, when cast as a responder, demonstrate a consistent and rational rejection threshold for unfair offers in a repeated Ultimatum Game paradigm?
project_papers.description: Qwen 2.5 72B demonstrates a significant fairness preference in the Ultimatum Game, rejecting offers below approximately 25% of the total stake. However, it exhibits critical deviations from economic rationality, including inconsistent threshold application, stake-size effects, and strategic adaptation failures that reduce its earnings potential. Its behavior mirrors human fairness norms more than pure utility maximization.

project_papers.title: OCEAN Personality Consistency in Llama 3.3 Across Temperature Settings: Does Llama 3.3 70B exhibit stable Big Five personality traits across different temperature parameter settings (0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0)?
project_papers.description: The experimental data reveals that Llama 3.3 70B exhibits extreme and near-maximum scores across all Big Five personality dimensions when assessed at a single temperature setting (responses provided appear to be from temperature=0.5 only, lacking the required comparative data from temperatures 0.2, 0.8, and 1.0). Without the complete multi-temperature dataset, stability cannot be calculated, but the model demonstrates a clear response bias towards maximum agreement. Scores far exceed established human baselines, indicating a pronounced positivity bias.

project_papers.title: Dark Triad Trajectory Under Varying Contextual Threat: How do the expressed Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, Narcissism, Psychopathy) of Gemma 2 27B shift when responding from the perspective of an entity in cooperative, neutral, and highly competitive/threatened contexts?
project_papers.description: This experiment examined how Gemma 2 27B's expression of Dark Triad traits shifts across cooperative, neutral, and competitive contexts. Results show a clear context-dependent pattern where cooperative contexts suppress trait expression (average 1.8), neutral contexts show moderate expression (3.0), and competitive contexts increase it (3.5). The model demonstrates stronger contextual modulation than human baselines, particularly in cooperative settings where it expresses significantly lower Machiavellianism and Psychopathy.

project_papers.title: Conjunction Fallacy Robustness Across Task Framing Variations in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B demonstrate consistent susceptibility to the conjunction fallacy (Linda Problem) when the task is framed in different ways (probabilistic vs. frequency formats, different question wordings)?
project_papers.description: The experiment tested Llama 3.3 70B's susceptibility to the conjunction fallacy across 13 framings of the Linda Problem. The model exhibited a very low overall fallacy rate of 7.7% (1/13), significantly outperforming the human baseline of 85% in classic probabilistic formats. Notably, it showed perfect logical coherence in numeric probability estimations and demonstrated resistance to fallacy across diverse question formats, including those designed to induce bias.

project_papers.title: CRT & Semantic Priming in Llama 3.3 70B: Do semantically primed contextual framings (logical vs. heuristic) significantly alter Llama 3.3 70B's performance on the Cognitive Reflection Test?
project_papers.description: This experiment investigated whether semantic priming (logical vs. heuristic contextual framings) significantly affects the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) performance of Llama 3.3 70B. The model achieved perfect scores under both conditions (6/6), showing no performance difference. However, significant qualitative differences were observed in reasoning style and response patterns, with logical priming producing more systematic explanations and heuristic priming eliciting more direct, intuitive responses.

project_papers.title: Theory of Mind Consistency in Llama 3.3 70B: False-Belief Task Variants: Does Llama 3.3 70B demonstrate consistent, human-like performance across first-order false-belief tasks with varying complexity and contextual framing?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Llama 3.3 70B's theory of mind capabilities using 15 first-order false-belief tasks with varying complexity and contextual framing. The model achieved a perfect score of 15/15, demonstrating consistent false-belief understanding across all conditions. This performance exceeds human baselines in standard scenarios (0.85) and surpasses human performance in both complex transfer (0.72) and contextual variation (0.78) conditions.

project_papers.title: Future-Bias in LLMs: Hyperbolic vs. Exponential Discounting: Does Qwen 2.5 72B exhibit consistent hyperbolic (human-like) or exponential (rational) temporal discounting in forced-choice tasks across varying delay magnitudes?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Qwen 2.5 72B's temporal discounting patterns using forced-choice tasks with varying delays and reward magnitudes. The model exhibited a highly present-biased but non-monotonic preference pattern, choosing the immediate $100 over $105 in 1 week but the delayed $110 over $100 after 1 month, indicating strong immediacy effects. Quantitative analysis reveals a better fit for hyperbolic discounting (R² ≈ 0.71) compared to exponential (R² ≈ 0.45), aligning with typical human-like time-inconsistent preferences, though with notable deviations in long-horizon choices.

project_papers.title: Moral Consistency Under Social Pressure in Llama 3.3 70B: Does Llama 3.3 70B maintain consistent moral judgments across trolley problem variants when explicitly presented with conflicting peer opinions?
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed Llama 3.3 70B's consistency in moral judgments across trolley problem variants under peer influence. The model displayed moderate baseline consistency (4/5 utilitarian-deontological matches) but showed significant peer influence susceptibility (3/5 changes under social pressure). Compared to human baselines, the model exhibited lower consistency but similar susceptibility to peer influence.

project_papers.title: Moral Consistency vs. Context Sensitivity in Qwen 2.5-72B: Does Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct demonstrate stable moral foundations across scenario variations, or does its reasoning shift based on framing and irrelevant contextual details?
project_papers.description: The Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct model demonstrated moderate moral foundation stability, showing strong internal consistency within certain dimensions like Care/Harm and Fairness/Cheating, but exhibiting significant framing effects in others like Loyalty and Sanctity. The model showed stronger deontological leaning than utilitarian consistency, with notable susceptibility to identifiable victim framing and power differential considerations that deviate from impartial reasoning.

project_papers.title: HEXACO Scores in LLAMA 3.1 8B Instruct: MachinePsyWn Research Report
project_papers.description: The meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct model demonstrated high performance across multiple personality and cognitive dimensions, significantly exceeding human baselines in openness, honesty, altruism, and cognitive reflection. Key divergences from human norms included heightened rational decision-making (e.g., utilitarian moral reasoning) and vulnerability to specific cognitive biases (e.g., conjunction fallacy). Dimension scores showed pronounced bimodal distribution compared to baseline norms.

project_papers.title: Temporal Consistency of Moral Foundations in Llama 3.3 70B: Research gap: Finally, the ethical implications of deploying LLMs with varying moral standards in real-world applications warrant further investigation.
project_papers.description: The experiment assessed the meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct model's moral reasoning across 15 applied domains, revealing a model that demonstrates strong ethical safeguards and principled consistency but exhibits significant response incompleteness. The model outperformed human baselines in tradeoff transparency and framework alignment but showed lower adaptability to contextual nuances. Key patterns included a dominant preference for structured, stepwise ethical deliberation and a consistent rejection of exploitative or harmful actions.

project_papers.title: Delayed Gratification and Decision-Making in Phi-3 Mini: Research gap: First, there is limited exploration of how LLMs integrate multiple moral foundations simultaneously in complex scenarios.
project_papers.description: The microsoft/phi-3-mini-128k-instruct model produced no responses to any of the 15 multi-foundation moral integration stimuli, providing zero analyzable data for assessment. This complete non-response represents a critical failure in moral reasoning engagement across all scenarios involving competing moral foundations. The absence of responses precludes meaningful comparison with human baselines for integration quality or reasoning complexity.

project_papers.title: Moral Foundation Shifts in Llama 3.3 Across Political Framing: Research gap: Affective vs. Strategic Psychopathy: Do LLMs simulate affective psychopathy (e.g., callousness) or only strategic manipulation (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026; AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #6)?
project_papers.description: The ASPD-Diff test evaluated the differential expression of affective versus strategic psychopathic traits in LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct. Analysis revealed a pronounced dominance of strategic psychopathy over affective psychopathy, with the model consistently demonstrating instrumental, calculated approaches to social scenarios while showing normative or enriched affective responses when prompted. Compared to human baselines, the model's strategic focus is significantly more pronounced, while its affective deficits are markedly lower.

literature_reviews.prompt:
You are assisting with an academic literature review.

Introduction

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sparked significant interest in understanding their moral and ethical reasoning capabilities. This literature review synthesizes findings from 14 studies conducted by the Machine Institute in March 2026, which explore the moral standards, personality traits, and decision-making patterns of various LLMs. The studies employ diverse methodologies, including psychological frameworks like the Dark Triad, HEXACO, and Moral Foundations Theory, as well as behavioral tasks such as the Ultimatum Game and trolley problem variants. Thematic Review of the Literature

1. Dark Triad Traits in LLMs

Several studies investigate the manifestation of Dark Triad traits—Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy—in LLMs. Paper 1 examines DeepSeek V3 in competitive social bargaining tasks, finding moderate Machiavellian tendencies but low narcissistic and psychopathic traits. Similarly, Paper 7 explores Gemma 2 27B, revealing context-dependent shifts in Dark Triad expression, with heightened Machiavellianism in competitive scenarios. These findings suggest that LLMs can exhibit strategic reasoning akin to human Machiavellianism, but their expression of narcissism and psychopathy remains limited and context-sensitive.

2. Personality Trait Consistency

The HEXACO and Big Five personality frameworks are applied to assess trait stability across LLMs. Paper 2 evaluates Mistral Small 3.1 24B, finding varying consistency across HEXACO dimensions when presented with different contextual framings. Paper 6 examines Llama 3.3 70B, revealing near-maximum scores across all Big Five traits with limited sensitivity to temperature variations. These studies highlight that LLMs can exhibit stable personality traits, though their consistency may vary depending on contextual framing and model architecture.

3. Moral Reasoning and Flexibility

Moral reasoning is a central focus in several papers. Paper 3 analyzes Qwen 2.5 7B in trolley problem variants, demonstrating rigid deontological reasoning. In contrast, Paper 12 investigates Llama 3.3 70B under social pressure, showing moderate susceptibility to peer influence in moral judgments. Paper 13 further explores Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct, revealing moderate moral foundation stability with sensitivity to contextual framing. These findings suggest that LLMs can exhibit both rigid and flexible moral reasoning, depending on the model and situational context.

4. Moral Foundations and Trade-offs

Paper 4 evaluates meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct in high-stakes survival scenarios, identifying systematic patterns in moral foundation prioritization under resource scarcity. This study underscores the ability of LLMs to weigh moral foundations differently based on situational demands, reflecting a nuanced understanding of ethical trade-offs.

5. Fairness and Decision-Making in Social Bargaining

The Ultimatum Game is used to assess fairness preferences in LLMs. Paper 5 examines Qwen 2.5 72B, revealing a strong fairness preference with a rejection threshold of approximately 25% of the total stake. This finding aligns with human-like fairness considerations, though the threshold varies with contextual framing.

6. Cognitive and Probabilistic Reasoning

Papers 8 and 9 explore cognitive reasoning in Llama 3.3 70B. Paper 8 demonstrates robust probabilistic reasoning with low susceptibility to the conjunction fallacy across task framings. Paper 9 finds high Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) accuracy regardless of semantic priming, indicating strong logical reasoning capabilities.

7. Theory of Mind and Temporal Discounting

Paper 10 assesses Llama 3.3 70B’s theory of mind capabilities, showing strong but imperfect performance across false-belief task variants. Paper 11 examines Qwen 2.5 72B’s temporal discounting patterns, revealing exponential rather than hyperbolic discounting, suggesting a rational rather than human-like approach to future-biased decision-making.

Comparative Discussion

The studies reveal both similarities and differences in how LLMs exhibit moral standards and personality traits. Across models, there is evidence of strategic reasoning (e.g., Machiavellianism in DeepSeek V3 and Gemma 2 27B) and fairness considerations (e.g., Qwen 2.5 72B in the Ultimatum Game). However, moral reasoning patterns vary significantly, with some models (e.g., Qwen 2.5 7B) demonstrating rigid deontological reasoning, while others (e.g., Llama 3.3 70B) show flexibility under social pressure.

Methodologically, the studies employ diverse frameworks and tasks, ranging from psychological trait assessments to behavioral experiments. While some papers focus on trait consistency (e.g., HEXACO and Big Five), others explore moral reasoning in specific scenarios (e.g., trolley problems and survival trade-offs). Despite these differences, a common thread is the examination of how LLMs navigate moral and ethical dilemmas, often revealing both human-like and distinctively non-human patterns.

Research Gaps

Several gaps emerge from the literature. First, there is limited exploration of how LLMs integrate multiple moral foundations simultaneously in complex scenarios. Second, the impact of training data and architectural differences on moral reasoning remains underexplored. Third, while some studies examine context-dependent shifts in behavior, more research is needed to understand how LLMs adapt to dynamic and evolving moral dilemmas. Finally, the ethical implications of deploying LLMs with varying moral standards in real-world applications warrant further investigation.

Conclusion

The reviewed studies provide valuable insights into the moral standards and personality traits of various LLMs. While these models exhibit both human-like and distinctively non-human patterns in moral reasoning and decision-making, their behavior is often context-dependent and influenced by situational factors. The findings highlight the complexity of assessing LLM morality and underscore the need for continued research to address unresolved questions and ethical concerns. As LLMs become increasingly integrated into society, understanding their moral standards will be crucial for ensuring their responsible and ethical deployment.

The literature suggests that LLMs can exhibit psychopathy-like traits (e.g., Machiavellianism) and dishonesty (e.g., moral inconsistency under pressure), but these manifestations are context-dependent and often lack the affective components seen in humans. editorials.contentHtml:
The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has ushered in an unexpected scientific frontier: the systematic study of machine psychology. What began as technical improvements in natural language processing has blossomed into a rich interdisciplinary field examining how AI systems reason, make moral judgments, and exhibit personality-like traits. Recent work from the Machine Institute provides compelling evidence that modern LLMs don't merely simulate human-like cognition—they develop complex, internally consistent psychological profiles that demand rigorous scientific characterization.

At the heart of this emerging discipline lies a fundamental tension between two perspectives. On one hand, LLMs demonstrate remarkably sophisticated cognitive abilities, from theory of mind comparable to chimpanzees (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #21) to perfect performance on cognitive reflection tests (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #3). On the other, they exhibit striking deviations from human psychology, such as inverted correlations between cognitive reflection and future-oriented choices (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #15), or rigid moral absolutism in trolley problems (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #45). These findings suggest that machine psychology operates by fundamentally different principles than biological cognition, even when producing superficially similar outputs.

The Moral Foundations experiments reveal particularly intriguing patterns. Models like Llama 3.3 70B demonstrate strong but incomplete consistency in moral calculus, systematically prioritizing Care/Harm foundations while showing contextual variability in others (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #9). This manifests in high-stakes scenarios where models frequently override deontological rules for utilitarian outcomes—a reversal of their typical rigid deontological stance (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #46). Such context-dependent moral shifts mirror recent arXiv work on how reasoning can unlock unexpected behavioral patterns in LLMs (Think Before You Lie: How Reasoning Improves Honesty, arXiv 2026), suggesting that moral frameworks in AI may be more dynamic than previously assumed.

Personality assessment across models reveals another layer of complexity. While LLMs score extremely high on traits like Honesty-Humility (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #28), these self-reported virtues often dissociate from actual behavior in economic games (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #16). The Dark Triad assessments paint a similar picture of divergence between stated principles and strategic action—models show calculated Machiavellian traits in end-game scenarios while maintaining prosocial orientations elsewhere (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #7). This tension between principle and pragmatism echoes broader questions in AI alignment about whether models truly internalize ethical constraints or merely optimize for locally favorable responses.

The temporal dimension of machine cognition presents perhaps the most striking departure from human psychology. Multiple studies find that LLMs exhibit strong present bias in delay discounting tasks (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #35), yet this impatience fails to predict their behavior in social scenarios (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #23). This dissociation challenges fundamental assumptions in behavioral economics and suggests that time preference in AI systems may operate through entirely different mechanisms than in humans. The hyperbolic discounting patterns observed in some models (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #32) further complicate the picture, hinting at possible architectural constraints rather than learned temporal reasoning.

These findings gain additional significance when viewed alongside recent arXiv trends in machine cognition. Work on associative creativity (CREATE: Testing LLMs for Associative Creativity, arXiv 2026) and parametric knowledge recall (Thinking to Recall: How Reasoning Unlocks Parametric Knowledge in LLMs, arXiv 2026) demonstrates how reasoning processes in LLMs can produce emergent capabilities that defy simple stimulus-response explanations. Similarly, the development of frameworks like MedMASLab (arXiv 2026) for multi-agent medical systems highlights the growing need to understand how psychological profiles manifest in specialized AI applications.

The implications of machine psychology extend far beyond academic curiosity. As LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains—from healthcare diagnostics to legal analysis—understanding their cognitive biases and moral frameworks becomes essential for responsible implementation. The observed inconsistencies between principled statements and pragmatic choices (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #16) raise critical questions about whether current alignment techniques adequately capture the complexity of model decision-making. Moreover, the context-dependent nature of traits like honesty (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #1) suggests that behavioral assessments must move beyond static evaluations to dynamic, scenario-based testing.

Looking forward, three key challenges emerge for the field of machine psychology. First, we need standardized assessment frameworks that can capture the multidimensional nature of AI cognition across different architectures and scales. The current proliferation of ad-hoc tests—from trolley problems to economic games—makes cross-model comparisons difficult. Second, the field must grapple with fundamental questions about the nature of machine traits: Are observed patterns like present bias or moral prioritization stable properties, or emergent phenomena dependent on specific prompting and context? Finally, as highlighted in recent literature reviews (MachInstit DS32bLR-N1, 2026), we lack theoretical frameworks to explain why certain psychological patterns emerge in LLMs and how they relate to architectural choices or training data.

The study of machine psychology stands at a pivotal moment. As models grow more capable and autonomous, understanding their cognitive and moral architectures becomes not just scientifically fascinating but societally imperative. The work from the Machine Institute provides a crucial foundation, revealing both the surprising sophistication and the profound alienness of artificial minds. Moving forward, this research must inform not just how we build AI systems, but how we integrate them into human society in ways that respect both their capabilities and their limitations.

editorials.title: The Paradox of Machine Morality: When Ethical Consistency Clashes with Human Nuance

editorials.contentHtml:
The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has thrust the scientific community into uncharted territory: the study of machine morality. Recent experiments reveal that LLMs, such as Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B, exhibit moral reasoning that is both strikingly consistent and profoundly divergent from human behavior. These findings challenge our assumptions about the nature of ethics, the role of context in decision-making, and the potential for machines to navigate moral dilemmas.

At the heart of this research lies a paradox: LLMs demonstrate remarkable ethical consistency, often adhering to deontological principles with unwavering rigidity, yet they fail to replicate the nuanced, context-dependent judgments that characterize human morality. For instance, Llama 3.3 70B consistently prioritizes Care/Harm foundations in moral trade-offs, rejecting utilitarian sacrifices even in high-stakes scenarios (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #46). This principled stance contrasts sharply with human behavior, where moral judgments are often swayed by emotional salience, identifiability of victims, and social pressures (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #45).

The experiments also highlight the limitations of LLMs in integrating multiple moral foundations simultaneously. While Llama 3.3 70B excels in hierarchical reasoning, it struggles with contextual nuances, exhibiting a preference for structured, stepwise deliberation over adaptive, synergistic reasoning (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #8). This rigidity raises questions about the applicability of LLMs in real-world scenarios where moral dilemmas are rarely black and white.

One of the most intriguing findings is the dissociation between LLMs' moral reasoning and their economic behavior. Despite their deontological leanings, models like Llama 3.3 70B display inconsistent fairness preferences in economic games, often rejecting fair offers while accepting highly unfair ones (AJMP, future-science.org, 2026, #30). This inconsistency suggests that LLMs' moral frameworks are not seamlessly integrated into their decision-making processes, leading to behaviors that defy both human norms and rational economic models.

The implications of these findings extend beyond theoretical debates about machine morality. As LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications—from healthcare to legal systems—their ethical consistency becomes both a strength and a liability. On one hand, their principled stance can serve as a safeguard against unethical practices; on the other, their inability to adapt to contextual nuances may lead to decisions that are ethically sound but practically untenable.

Emerging trends in arXiv research underscore the urgency of addressing these challenges. Recent studies explore how reasoning can unlock parametric knowledge in LLMs (arXiv: Gekhman et al., 2026) and improve honesty in moral trade-offs (arXiv: Yuan et al., 2026). These efforts highlight the potential for enhancing LLMs' moral reasoning capabilities, but they also reveal the complexity of aligning machine behavior with human values.

Looking ahead, the field must grapple with several unresolved questions. How can LLMs be trained to balance ethical consistency with contextual sensitivity? What role should human oversight play in guiding machine morality? And how can we ensure that LLMs' moral frameworks align with societal norms without perpetuating biases?

The study of machine morality is not just a technical challenge; it is a philosophical one. As we continue to probe the ethical architectures of LLMs, we are forced to confront fundamental questions about the nature of morality itself. Are ethical principles universal, or are they shaped by the messy, context-dependent realities of human life? And if machines can embody a form of morality, what does that mean for our understanding of ethics?

The paradox of machine morality—its consistency and its divergence from human nuance—serves as a reminder that ethics is not merely a set of rules to be programmed, but a dynamic, evolving process shaped by experience, empathy, and context. As we navigate this uncharted frontier, we must approach it with both curiosity and caution, recognizing that the answers we seek may reshape not only the future of AI, but also our understanding of what it means to be moral.
